topics.title: Endocrine glands, hormones and the human endocrine system

learn.hook: A few micrograms of a hormone can change your heart rate, mood or growth. Tiny messengers, giant effects.
points: Endocrine glands lack ducts, so they are called ductless glands; their secretions are hormones, released into the blood.

Classical definition: a hormone is a chemical produced by endocrine glands, released into blood and carried to a distant target organ. Current definition: hormones are non-nutrient chemicals that act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts; this also covers molecules from non-gland tissues.
Invertebrates have very simple endocrine systems with few hormones; in vertebrates, a large number of chemicals act as hormones and provide coordination.
Organised endocrine bodies in humans: pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus and gonads (testes in males, ovaries in females).
Other organs such as the gastrointestinal tract, liver, kidney and heart also produce hormones.

example.q: Why is the pancreas called both an exocrine and an endocrine gland while the thyroid is only endocrine?
steps: The pancreas releases digestive juice through a duct (exocrine) and hormones into blood from the islets (endocrine).
The thyroid releases its hormones only into blood; it has no duct.
example.answer: The pancreas has both duct and ductless secretions; the thyroid only ductless.

learn.reallife: India's iodised salt programme, one of the world's largest public health successes, targets a single endocrine gland: the thyroid.

topics.title: The hypothalamus and the pituitary gland

learn.hook: The pituitary is called the 'master gland', but it takes orders from its boss just above it: the hypothalamus.
points: The hypothalamus, the basal part of the diencephalon (forebrain), has groups of neurosecretory cells called nuclei that produce hormones regulating pituitary secretion.

Hypothalamic hormones are releasing hormones (stimulate pituitary secretion, e.g. GnRH stimulates gonadotrophin release) and inhibiting hormones (e.g. somatostatin inhibits growth hormone release). They pass along axons, are released at nerve endings and reach the anterior pituitary through a portal circulatory system. The posterior pituitary is under direct neural regulation of the hypothalamus.
The pituitary sits in a bony cavity, the sella turcica, attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk. It has an adenohypophysis (pars distalis and pars intermedia) and a neurohypophysis (pars nervosa).

Pars distalis (anterior pituitary) produces GH, prolactin (PRL), TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH. Pars intermedia secretes melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH); in humans it is almost merged with the pars distalis.
The neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin, which are actually made in the hypothalamus and transported along axons.

example.q: Which pituitary hormones are actually made in the hypothalamus, and how do they reach the pituitary?
steps: Oxytocin and vasopressin are made by hypothalamic neurons.
They travel along axons to the neurohypophysis, where they are stored and released.
example.answer: Oxytocin and vasopressin; carried axonally to the posterior pituitary.

learn.reallife: Endocrinologists at Indian hospitals treat pituitary tumours that can over-produce hormones such as growth hormone or prolactin.

topics.title: Functions and disorders of pituitary hormones

learn.hook: Too much growth hormone in childhood can make a person over 7 feet tall; too little, and growth stays stunted.
points: Growth hormone (GH): over-secretion in children causes gigantism; low secretion causes pituitary dwarfism. Excess in adults, especially in middle age, causes acromegaly: severe disfigurement, especially of the face; it is hard to diagnose early and can lead to serious complications if unchecked.

Prolactin regulates growth of mammary glands and milk formation. TSH stimulates synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones. ACTH stimulates synthesis and secretion of glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex.

LH and FSH stimulate the gonads (gonadotrophins). In males, LH stimulates androgen secretion from the testis; FSH and androgens regulate spermatogenesis. In females, LH induces ovulation of mature Graafian follicles and maintains the corpus luteum; FSH stimulates growth and development of ovarian follicles. MSH regulates skin pigmentation.
Oxytocin stimulates contraction of smooth muscles: in females, vigorous uterine contraction at childbirth and milk ejection from mammary glands.

Vasopressin (ADH) acts on the kidney, stimulating reabsorption of water and electrolytes by distal tubules and reducing water loss (diuresis). Impaired ADH synthesis or release leads to water loss and dehydration: diabetes insipidus.

example.q: A patient passes huge volumes of dilute urine and is always thirsty, but blood sugar is normal. Which hormone may be deficient?
steps: Normal blood sugar rules out diabetes mellitus.
Large volumes of dilute urine mean the kidney cannot conserve water.
This happens when ADH (vasopressin) is lacking: diabetes insipidus.
example.answer: ADH (vasopressin); the condition is diabetes insipidus.

learn.reallife: Doctors in Indian hospitals give synthetic oxytocin to help uterine contractions during childbirth and to reduce bleeding after delivery.

learn.hook: Before iodised salt, goitre (a swollen neck) was common in the Himalayan foothills. A pinch of iodine changed that.
points: The pineal gland on the dorsal side of the forebrain secretes melatonin, which regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm: the sleep-wake cycle and body temperature. It also influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle and defence capability.

The thyroid has two lobes on either side of the trachea joined by a thin flap of connective tissue, the isthmus. It is made of follicles and stromal tissue; follicular cells make tetraiodothyronine or thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃). Iodine is essential for normal hormone synthesis.

Iodine deficiency causes hypothyroidism and goitre (enlarged thyroid). Hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development of the baby: stunted growth (cretinism), impaired mental development, low IQ, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism. In adult women it may make the menstrual cycle irregular.

Hyperthyroidism (from thyroid cancer or nodules) raises hormone levels abnormally. Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism with an enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, increased basal metabolic rate and weight loss.

Thyroid hormones regulate basal metabolic rate, support RBC formation, control metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, and influence water and electrolyte balance. The thyroid also secretes thyrocalcitonin (TCT), a protein hormone regulating blood calcium.

example.q: How many iodine atoms are in one molecule each of T₄ and T₃ together?
steps: T₄ (tetraiodothyronine) has 4 iodine atoms.
T₃ (triiodothyronine) has 3 iodine atoms.
Total = 4 + 3 = 7.

learn.reallife: Under India's National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme, iodised salt is promoted nationwide to prevent goitre and cretinism.

learn.hook: Four rice-grain-sized glands behind your thyroid decide whether your bones give up calcium to your blood. They work hand in hand with the thyroid's TCT.
points: There are four parathyroid glands on the back side of the thyroid, one pair in each of its two lobes. They secrete a peptide hormone, parathyroid hormone (PTH); its secretion is regulated by circulating Ca²⁺ levels.

PTH increases blood Ca²⁺: it stimulates bone resorption (dissolution or demineralisation), stimulates reabsorption of Ca²⁺ by renal tubules and increases Ca²⁺ absorption from digested food. So PTH is a hypercalcaemic hormone. With TCT, it plays a major role in calcium balance.
The thymus is a lobular structure on the dorsal side of the heart and the aorta. It plays a major role in development of the immune system.
It secretes peptide hormones called thymosins, which play a major role in differentiation of T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity) and promote antibody production (humoral immunity).
The thymus degenerates in old individuals, decreasing thymosin production, so immune responses of old people become weak.

example.q: Blood calcium falls. Name the gland that responds, the hormone, and three ways it raises calcium.
steps: Parathyroid glands secrete PTH when Ca²⁺ falls.
PTH causes bone resorption.
It increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption in renal tubules.
It increases Ca²⁺ absorption from digested food.
example.answer: Parathyroid → PTH → bone resorption, renal reabsorption, intestinal absorption

learn.reallife: Elderly people in India are more prone to infections partly because the thymus shrinks with age, weakening T-cell production.

learn.hook: A dog barks suddenly at night and your heart pounds, your pupils widen and your hair stands up. That's adrenaline, the 'fight or flight' hormone.
points: A pair of adrenal glands sits one at the anterior part of each kidney. Each has a central adrenal medulla and an outer adrenal cortex.

The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), the catecholamines. They are secreted rapidly in stress and emergencies (emergency hormones, hormones of fight or flight): they increase alertness, pupil dilation, piloerection (raising of hairs) and sweating; increase heart rate, strength of heart contraction and breathing rate; and stimulate breakdown of glycogen (raising blood glucose), lipids and proteins.

The adrenal cortex has three layers: zona reticularis (inner), zona fasciculata (middle) and zona glomerulosa (outer). It secretes corticoids. Glucocorticoids (mainly cortisol) act on carbohydrate metabolism: they stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis, inhibit cellular uptake and use of amino acids, help maintain cardiovascular and kidney functions, produce anti-inflammatory reactions, suppress the immune response and stimulate RBC production.

Mineralocorticoids (mainly aldosterone) regulate water and electrolytes: aldosterone acts on renal tubules to reabsorb Na⁺ and water and excrete K⁺ and phosphate, maintaining electrolytes, body fluid volume, osmotic pressure and blood pressure.

Small amounts of androgenic steroids from the cortex help growth of axial, pubic and facial hair at puberty. Underproduction of cortical hormones alters carbohydrate metabolism, causing acute weakness and fatigue: Addison's disease.

example.q: List the layers of the adrenal cortex from outside inwards and the main hormone class of the outer layer.
steps: Outer: zona glomerulosa.
Middle: zona fasciculata.
Inner: zona reticularis.
The zona glomerulosa is associated with mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone.
example.answer: Zona glomerulosa → zona fasciculata → zona reticularis

learn.reallife: Adrenaline auto-injectors are carried by people with severe allergies, and doctors in Indian emergency rooms use adrenaline in cardiac arrest and anaphylaxis.

learn.hook: India has one of the largest numbers of people with diabetes in the world. At the heart of the disease are tiny islands of cells in the pancreas.
points: The pancreas is a composite gland, both exocrine and endocrine. The endocrine part is the islets of Langerhans: about 1 to 2 million islets, only 1 to 2% of pancreatic tissue.
Islets have α-cells (secrete glucagon) and β-cells (secrete insulin).

Glucagon, a peptide hormone, acts mainly on liver cells (hepatocytes): it stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and reduces cellular glucose uptake, raising blood sugar (hyperglycaemia). So glucagon is a hyperglycaemic hormone.

Insulin, a peptide hormone, acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes: it enhances cellular glucose uptake and utilisation, lowering blood glucose (hypoglycaemia), and stimulates conversion of glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis). Insulin and glucagon together maintain glucose homeostasis.
Prolonged hyperglycaemia leads to diabetes mellitus, with loss of glucose in urine and formation of harmful ketone bodies. Diabetic patients are successfully treated with insulin therapy.

example.q: After a sweet-heavy Diwali meal, blood glucose rises. Which islet cells respond, with which hormone, and what does it do?
steps: High blood glucose stimulates β-cells.
β-cells release insulin.
Insulin increases glucose uptake by liver and fat cells and stimulates glycogenesis, lowering blood glucose.
example.answer: β-cells; insulin; increases glucose uptake and glycogenesis.

learn.reallife: Indian pharma companies produce insulin at scale, and the national NCD screening programme checks adults for diabetes at health and wellness centres.

topics.title: Gonads as endocrine glands: testis and ovary

learn.hook: At puberty, a voice deepens or rises, and the body changes in many ways. The messengers behind these changes come from the testes and ovaries.
points: The testes, a pair in the scrotal sac, are primary sex organs and endocrine glands. They have seminiferous tubules and stromal (interstitial) tissue.

Leydig (interstitial) cells in the intertubular spaces produce androgens, mainly testosterone. Androgens regulate development, maturation and functions of male accessory sex organs (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, urethra); stimulate muscular growth, growth of facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness and low pitch of voice; play a major stimulatory role in spermatogenesis; influence male sexual behaviour (libido) through the CNS; and have anabolic effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.

The ovaries, a pair in the abdomen, are primary female sex organs producing one ovum in each menstrual cycle, and two groups of steroid hormones: oestrogen and progesterone. They have ovarian follicles and stromal tissue.

Oestrogen is mainly made by growing ovarian follicles. It stimulates growth and activities of female secondary sex organs, development of growing follicles, appearance of female secondary sex characters (e.g. high pitch of voice), and mammary gland development; it also regulates female sexual behaviour.

After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which mainly secretes progesterone. Progesterone supports pregnancy and acts on mammary glands to stimulate formation of alveoli (milk-storing sacs) and milk secretion.

example.q: Which structure secretes progesterone, and where does it come from?
steps: After ovulation, the ruptured Graafian follicle changes into the corpus luteum.
The corpus luteum mainly secretes progesterone.
example.answer: The corpus luteum, formed from the ruptured follicle after ovulation.

learn.reallife: School health and life-skills programmes in India explain puberty changes clinically and respectfully, linking them to hormones from the testes and ovaries.

topics.title: Hormones of the heart, kidney and gut

learn.hook: Your stomach, intestine, heart and kidney aren't classified as endocrine glands, yet each sends out hormones every day.
points: The atrial wall of the heart secretes atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), a peptide hormone. When BP rises, ANF causes dilation of blood vessels, reducing blood pressure.
Juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce erythropoietin, a peptide hormone that stimulates erythropoiesis (RBC formation).

Endocrine cells of the gastrointestinal tract secrete four major peptide hormones. Gastrin acts on gastric glands to stimulate secretion of HCl and pepsinogen. Secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas to stimulate secretion of water and bicarbonate ions.
Cholecystokinin (CCK) acts on the pancreas and gall bladder to stimulate secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice. Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) inhibits gastric secretion and motility.
Several non-endocrine tissues secrete growth factors, essential for normal growth of tissues and their repair or regeneration.

example.q: Fatty food enters the duodenum. Which gut hormone releases bile and pancreatic enzymes?
steps: Bile comes from the gall bladder; enzymes from the pancreas.
Cholecystokinin acts on both.

learn.reallife: Patients with chronic kidney disease in India often become anaemic because damaged kidneys make less erythropoietin; synthetic erythropoietin injections help.

learn.hook: Insulin knocks on the cell's door and sends a message inside; steroid hormones walk right in and talk to the genes.
points: Hormones act by binding specific proteins called hormone receptors, present only in target tissues. Receptors on the cell membrane are membrane-bound receptors; those inside the cell are intracellular receptors, mostly nuclear receptors. Each receptor is specific to one hormone.
Binding forms a hormone-receptor complex, which causes biochemical changes in the target tissue and so regulates its metabolism and physiological functions.

By chemical nature: peptide, polypeptide and protein hormones (insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones); steroids (cortisol, testosterone, oestradiol, progesterone); iodothyronines (thyroid hormones); amino-acid derivatives (epinephrine).
Hormones acting on membrane-bound receptors normally do not enter the cell; they generate second messengers (e.g. cyclic AMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺) that regulate cellular metabolism.

Hormones acting on intracellular receptors (steroids, iodothyronines) mostly regulate gene expression or chromosome function through the hormone-receptor complex interacting with the genome, causing physiological and developmental effects. Hormone levels are kept in check by feedback: e.g. a rise in body fluid volume switches off osmoreceptors and suppresses ADH release.

example.q: Classify insulin and cortisol by chemical nature and by type of receptor.
steps: Insulin is a peptide hormone; it cannot cross the lipid membrane, so it binds membrane-bound receptors and uses second messengers.
Cortisol is a steroid; it enters the cell and binds intracellular (nuclear) receptors, regulating gene expression.
example.answer: Insulin: peptide, membrane receptor, second messengers. Cortisol: steroid, intracellular receptor, gene expression.

learn.reallife: Many modern drugs developed and made in India are designed to block or mimic hormone receptors, such as drugs for diabetes and hormone-sensitive cancers.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
